comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: same data modality (10-K reports) and SVM regression framework; Difference: Kogan uses raw bag-of-words; current paper augments lexicon with embedding-aware IR weights.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript references and SHARED_ANALYSIS (References list; Introduction)

comparable_works.relevance: Lexicon-based sentiment baseline using Loughran & McDonald lexicon; directly compared in experiments (Table 2).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: lexicon-based sentiment aggregated into regression; Difference: Wang uses TC weights without embedding-augmented IR weighting; current paper reports higher r2.
comparable_works.source_trace: Paper's Baselines section and Table 2

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work that used Word2Vec to expand the financial lexicon—closest apparent precedent for embedding-driven lexicon expansion.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both use Word2Vec expansions of lexicon terms; Difference: Tsai & Wang expand the lexicon (add neighbors) while this paper injects embedding similarity directly into term counts and IR weight formulas (t̂cdi), a different conceptual framing.
comparable_works.source_trace: Related Work section and Methodology 4.1 (LexExt described); SHARED_ANALYSIS

comparable_works.relevance: Technical precedent for extending IR weighting with word-embedding similarity (the exact technique the authors adapt from retrieval literature).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: same embedding-aware weighting formula and threshold rationale; Difference: prior work focused on retrieval/ranking; current work repurposes mechanism for sentiment feature construction and regression forecasting.
comparable_works.source_trace: Methodology 4.1 eq.3 and References

comparable_works.relevance: Representative work on temporal changes in language models/dynamics, relevant background for concept drift/temporal selection reasoning.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both address changing language and time-evolving textual signals; Difference: Yogatama et al. focus on streaming language-model adaptation, while paper uses centroid clustering to select training window.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved literature 'Dynamic Language Models for Streaming Text' in retrieval context

uncertainty_flags: Absence of fold-level variances or confidence intervals for r2/MSE comparisons (major uncertainty about robustness).
Potential temporal/company-level leakage in CV and PCA/Word2Vec fitting could inflate reported performance.
Dependence on specific embedding hyperparameters and threshold (0.70) without sensitivity analysis (uncertain generality).
Risk-factor extraction heuristics not validated against ground truth (uncertainty in feature purity).
Choice to use 2012–2015 cluster reduces dataset size; uncertain how well models generalize to truly future (post-2015) reports.
alternative_interpretations: The observed improvements may mainly stem from denser feature representations induced by expansion + PCA rather than semantic correctness of expansion; simple co-occurrence smoothing or dimensionality-enrichment techniques might obtain similar gains.

Temporal cluster selection benefits could be due to removing outlier years with extreme market regimes (e.g., 2008 crisis) rather than purely language concept drift—thus gains may partly come from label distribution shifts.

Stacking improvements may arise from ensembling regularization rather than superior modality fusion; MKL underperformance could be due to suboptimal MKL hyperparameters or kernel choices rather than a structural weakness of MKL.
Sector-specific underperformance versus general model might reflect overfitting in sector models or covariate shift in features rather than only sample-size scarcity.
transparency_notes: Word2Vec training details (window size, vector dimension, negative sampling, epochs) are not fully documented; authors should provide training scripts/params for reproducibility.
Unclear whether PCA and Word2Vec were trained inside CV folds (correct) or on full dataset (incorrect)—need explicit pipeline order.
The corpus and code availability: manuscript mentions dataset available at anonymous URL but does not indicate code release for t̂cdi construction and stacking splits.
No reporting of per-fold results or seeds; providing these would increase reproducibility and enable independent verification.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The approach adapts embedding-augmented IR weighting from retrieval to sentiment/regression forecasting; sparse direct precedent exists in volatility forecasting literature (Tsai & Wang expanded lexicons, Rekabsaz operated in IR). Sparse precedents should be construed as a plausible innovation opportunity but not as validation of empirical robustness—novelty is orthogonal to careful methodological verification.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If Word2Vec neighbors reliably capture sentiment-preserving synonyms within the 10-K genre (low antonymy), then t̂cdi will enrich signal and improve prediction.
If PCA is fit strictly within training folds and preserves predictive directions, the embedding-augmented enriched features will generalize; poor cross-fold PCA would instead leak information.

If temporal selection genuinely reduces semantic drift (rather than just removing noisy years with atypical labels), models trained on recent clusters will maintain performance on future reports; otherwise, performance will degrade when language evolves post-2015.
If sector term-sense disambiguation yields consistent within-sector semantics and sufficient per-sector data accrues, sector-specific models should eventually outperform general models.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Promising conceptual transfer with limited prior analogs in forecasting literature
novelty_lenses.rationale: The adaptation of embedding-aware IR weighting (t̂cdi) to sentiment feature construction is a clear conceptual move that reframes lexicon expansion as count-propagation rather than simple lexicon growth; Rekabsaz provided technical precedent in IR, but applying it to volatility prediction is novel and coherent.
evidence: Methodology 4.1 eq.3 and cited Rekabsaz et al.; experimental gains in Table 1/2.
uncertainty_flags: Outcome depends on embedding quality and lack of sensitivity analyses leaves generality uncertain.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Innovative and practically useful observation but needs stronger causal/robustness support
novelty_lenses.rationale: Year-centroid clustering and the decision to restrict training to a recent coherent cluster is an operationally useful strategy to mitigate concept drift; however, the basis for selecting cluster boundaries and the risk of overfitting to a recent window warrant further formalization and testing.
evidence: Figure 1a heatmap and Figure 1b plot showing r2 improvements when dropping older years.
uncertainty_flags: Clustering representation choice and confounding with label regime shifts leave interpretation open.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Stacking improves r2 and temporal stability per presented results; the paper should disentangle whether gains come from complementary signal or simply ensemble variance reduction.
evidence: Table 1 stacking vs MKL vs early fusion; Figure 2a stability gains.
uncertainty_flags: No ablation showing base-model calibration/overlap or stacking meta-model coefficients reduces interpretive clarity.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately to highly confident in the factual summary and in the methodological concerns listed because they reference explicit missing details (CIs, pipeline ordering, hyperparameter sweeps) present across the Methods/Experiments sections. The interval reflects uncertainty about the generalizability of the empirical gains (which depend on unstated implementation details and sensitivity analysis).

prior_stage_inputs: SHARED_ANALYSIS (extracted claims, assumptions, argument focus, evaluation targets, uncertainty flags)
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper adapts embedding-augmented IR term-weighting (extend tcdi by cosine-weighted counts of Word2Vec neighbors, threshold 0.70) to build document-level sentiment features from 10-K Item 1A Risk Factors, reduces them with PCA (chosen 400 dims), uses SVM-RBF regressors, and combines text with market features via early fusion, MKL, and stacking. Empirically (5-fold CV on SEC 2012–2015 subset, n=3892 reports), the embedding-extended weightings (notably B̂M25) outperform standard weightings and prior lexicon-expansion baselines (Wang 2013, Tsai & Wang 2014) on first-year volatility (r2: Text our method 0.439 vs Tsai 0.395; Text+Market our 0.527 vs baselines 0.484–0.499). Stacking improves fusion performance relative to MKL and early fusion. Temporal centroid analysis motivates using 2012–2015 due to apparent concept drift, and sectoral analyses show distinct term-sense patterns but sector-specific models do not beat the general model—likely due to smaller per-sector training sizes. The chain of reasoning is coherent and supported by tables/figures, but important methodological gaps weaken causal attribution: missing fold-level variances/CIs/statistical tests, potential temporal/data-leakage in embedding/PCA fitting, limited sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters (Word2Vec, similarity threshold, top-k neighbors, PCA dims, SVM tuning), and under-validated Risk Factors extraction and outlier filtering. I classify individual claims as supported, partially supported, or overstated below with evidence and uncertainty flags.
logical_argument_graph: A: 10-K Risk Factors contain risk-relevant language useful for volatility forecasting -> evidence: prior literature (Kogan et al., Wang et al.), authors' dataset and performance gains when using text.

B: Word2Vec on the corpus yields meaningful term similarities -> evidence: authors train Word2Vec on corpus and cite Rekabsaz for threshold choice; risk: embedding hyperparams and training leakage unspecified.

C: Extending tcdi to t̂cdi via cosine-weighted similar-token counts improves IR weighting (T̂*, B̂M25) -> evidence: eq.3 definition, Table 1 showing hat-variants outperform basic forms; risk: no CI/stat tests, hyperparameter sensitivity.

D: PCA(400) yields tractable dense features preserving signal -> evidence: authors state preliminary sweep 50–1000 dims and selected 400; risk: selection process not detailed and fitted possibly on full data.
E: SVM-RBF (C=1, epsilon=0.1) is appropriate learner -> evidence: prior studies used similar; risk: tuning details and fairness across baselines ambiguous.

F: Stacking (late fusion) combining text and market yields further gains and longer-horizon stability -> evidence: Table 1/2 and Figure 2a show higher point r2 and slower decay; risk: no uncertainty intervals and small meta-training split concerns.

G: Temporal centroid clustering (2006–2008, 2009–2011, 2012–2015) indicates concept drift; restricting to recent cluster improves results -> evidence: Figure 1a (centroid cosine heatmap) and Figure 1b (r2 improves when older years dropped); risk: representation choice and lack of formal drift tests.

H: Sectors show distinct term-senses but sector-specific models underperform general model due to limited data -> evidence: Figures 2c, 3a/3b, term examples (fire, beneficial); risk: causality (sample size vs domain mismatch) not fully separated.

evidence: Definition and implementation of t̂cdi(t) in eq.3, using cosine similarity threshold 0.70.
Table 1: hat-variants (B̂M25, T̂C) show higher point r2 than non-hat counterparts.
Table 2: Our method (Text r2 0.439) > Tsai (0.395) and Wang (0.345) under 5-fold CV on 2012–2015 subset.
uncertainty_flags: No confidence intervals, p-values, or per-fold variances reported for r2 differences (statistical significance unknown).
Word2Vec training details (vector size, window, epochs), whether embeddings were trained inside CV folds or on whole corpus, and sensitivity to threshold=0.70 and top-20 neighbors are not provided.
Possible leakage: if Word2Vec and PCA are fitted on full dataset prior to CV splits, feature leakage could inflate performance.

identified_claims.claim_label: text+market fusion via stacking yields further gains
identified_claims.claim_text: Combining textual features derived from 10-K Risk Factors with market-derived features using stacking yields additional predictive performance and produces more stable long-horizon predictions than market features alone.
evidence: Stacking described: 70%-30% split to train base models then SVM-RBF meta-model.
Table 2: Text+Market Our method r2 = 0.527 > Market alone r2 = 0.485 and Text alone r2 = 0.439.
Figure 2a: visual quartile curves show Text+Market above Market and decaying less rapidly.

identified_claims.claim_text: Reports from recent years (2012–2015) form more coherent clusters and models trained on this recent cluster provide better volatility prediction performance than models trained including older years due to conceptual drift.
evidence: Figure 1a: cosine-similarity heatmap shows three year-clusters (2006–08, 2009–11, 2012–15).
Figure 1b: r2 increases as older years are progressively dropped; authors choose 2012–2015 subset (3892 reports).
uncertainty_flags: Clustering uses feature centroids from Tsai & Wang representation; alternative representations might yield different clusters.
No formal concept-drift test or held-out future-year generalization beyond limited train-on-past experiments; selecting data post-hoc risks optimistic evaluation (temporal selection bias).

identified_claims.claim_text: The best-performing pipeline uses B̂M25 weighting with LexExt lexicon, PCA to 400 dimensions, SVM-RBF base learners, and stacking for fusion; this configuration achieves the reported top results.

evidence: Authors report initial PCA sweep and selection of 400 dims; B̂M25+LexExt reported best among tested combinations in Table 1.
Stacking chosen as best fusion in Table 1; final results in Table 2 reported for B̂M25 + LexExt + PCA(400)+Stacking.

SVM hyperparameters fixed by prior studies; no hyperparameter search per method reported, raising fairness concerns.
No ablation isolating PCA effect (i.e., raw sparse features with appropriate regularization) to confirm PCA necessity.

identified_claims.claim_label: sectoral patterns exist but sector-specific models underperform
identified_claims.claim_text: Different financial sectors exhibit distinct risk-term patterns and term-sense disambiguations, but sector-specific models trained on available per-sector data do not outperform a general model—likely due to limited per-sector training data; sector-aware analysis still reveals interpretable term importances.
evidence: Figure 2c shows varying per-sector r2; Figures 3a/3b compare sector-specific vs general vs sector-agnostic same-size sample showing sector-specific underperforming general model.
Linear-regression coefficient examples: 'fire' high in energy sector; 'beneficial' negative in health/basic industries due to 'beneficial owner' contexts.

Interpretability via coefficients likely affected by stemming, multicollinearity, and PCA absence—no confidence intervals for coefficients provided.

identified_claims.claim_text: Text-derived features provide a more stable predictive signal over longer horizons compared to market-only models; fusing text with market features reduces performance decay at longer horizons.
evidence: Figure 2a quartile plot showing GARCH and Market curves decay faster than Text; Text+Market track higher and decay less.
Authors' explanation: historical prices become less relevant over time while textual signals remain informative.
uncertainty_flags: No confidence bands or statistical tests for quartile differences; visual differences may be sample-specific.
Quartile window choice (64 trading days) is conventional but alternative horizons might change comparative decay behavior.

strengths.title: Coherent adaptation of embedding-augmented IR to long-form sentiment
strengths.description: The paper describes a clear, mechanistic adaptation (eq.3) of IR weighting to add cosine-weighted counts from Word2Vec neighbors, with mapping to several standard weightings (TC/TF/TFIDF/BM25) and explicit formulae.
evidence: Methodology Section 4.1 defines t̂cdi(t) and hat-variants; direct citation of Rekabsaz et al. for thresholding.

strengths.title: Comprehensive empirical comparisons
strengths.description: Authors compare many permutations: multiple weighting schemes, lexicon variants (Lex vs LexExt), fusion strategies (early, stacking, MKL), and baselines (GARCH, Market, Wang, Tsai), providing an extensive empirical landscape.
evidence: Tables 1 and 2; Figures 2 and 3; explicit replication of prior baselines (Wang 2013, Tsai 2014).

strengths.title: Temporal and sectoral characterization adds interpretive depth
strengths.description: The paper goes beyond point prediction to analyze temporal centroid clustering, effect of training window selection, and per-sector term-sense examples, offering dataset insights valuable to the community.
evidence: Figure 1a/1b (year-centroid similarity and performance vs year-range) and sector analyses in Section 6.3 with term examples.

concerns.title: Missing statistical uncertainty and fold-level reporting
concerns.description: Key comparisons (Tables 1 and 2, quartile curves) present only point estimates (average r2 and MSE) without per-fold variances, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests; this prevents assessing robustness of reported improvements.
evidence: Tables present means only; SHARED_ANALYSIS and prior reviewers note absence of CI/p-values/variance information.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report per-fold r2/MSE (all folds), provide standard errors and 95% CIs, and run appropriate paired tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank or bootstrap) comparing key configurations (e.g., B̂M25 vs BM25; Text+Market stacking vs Market baseline).

concerns.title: Potential temporal/data leakage in embedding and PCA fitting
concerns.description: Word2Vec and PCA appear trained on the entire 2012–2015 corpus prior to cross-validation, but the paper does not state whether embeddings/PCA were fitted inside CV folds or only on training folds—if fitted on all data this can leak future information into features and inflate performance.
evidence: Method describes Word2Vec built on corpus of all reports and PCA chosen based on initial experiments, but CV fitting protocol for embedding/PCA not specified (Sections 4.1, 5).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify and, if needed, re-run experiments ensuring all representation learning (Word2Vec, PCA) is fitted only on training data within each CV or temporal split; report differences. If computationally heavy, report an experiment with time-ordered splits where embedding/PCA are trained on past-only data.

concerns.title: Insufficient sensitivity analyses for embedding and expansion hyperparameters
concerns.description: Core claim C1 depends on embedding-based expansion (threshold 0.70, top-20 neighbors) and Word2Vec hyperparameters; only a single threshold/top-k and Word2Vec training description is given without ablation to show robustness.
evidence: Eq.3 uses threshold=0.70 per Rekabsaz; LexExt described as top-20 neighbors; authors cite Rekabsaz but do not vary these settings in experiments.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run sensitivity sweeps across similarity thresholds (e.g., 0.60–0.80), neighbor counts (5, 10, 20, 50), and at least one alternative embedding (GloVe or fastText) or varying Word2Vec dims; report impact on r2 and variance.

concerns.title: Risk Factors extraction and label filtering under-validated
concerns.description: Extraction of Item 1A Risk Factors uses term-matching heuristics and volatility labels are filtered by mean ± 3 std; neither extraction accuracy nor the potential impact of outlier removal is quantified.
evidence: Section 5: statement about heuristics and ±3σ filtering; no validation vs manual annotations or sensitivity analysis reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide precision/recall estimates of Risk Factors extraction on a manually annotated subset (e.g., 100 reports). Analyze model performance with and without outlier filtering and report whether extreme volatility cases alter conclusions.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter tuning and fairness across baselines
concerns.description: SVM hyperparameters (C, epsilon, kernel) are fixed by prior studies but it's unclear whether baselines and proposed models had comparable hyperparameter searches; lack of tuning transparency risks unfair comparisons.
evidence: Section 4.1 sets C=1.0, epsilon=0.1, RBF chosen from 'initial experiments' but no tuning grid or per-method validation described.
Baselines (GARCH, Market, Wang, Tsai) may need different optimal hyperparameters.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Describe and/or perform hyperparameter searches (nested CV or grid) for each model class and baseline, report chosen values and whether conclusions hold under tuned settings.

concerns.title: Causal attribution for sector-specific underperformance is incomplete
concerns.description: Authors attribute sector-specific model underperformance to sample size (plausible) but do not provide learning curves or controlled cross-sector transfer experiments to separate sample-size from domain mismatch or model capacity issues.
evidence: Figures 3a/3b include sector-agnostic same-size sampling which suggests sample size effect, but no learning curves or transfer experiments are presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add learning-curve plots per sector (performance vs training size) and cross-sector transfer tests (train on sector A, test on B) to isolate causes; consider simple domain-adaptation baselines.

uncertainty_flags: No reported confidence intervals, per-fold variances, or formal significance testing for r2/MSE comparisons.
Word2Vec and PCA training protocols relative to CV folds are unspecified — risk of temporal or label leakage.
Hyperparameters (Word2Vec dims/window, threshold 0.70, top-20 neighbors, PCA dims, SVM params, stacking split) lack sensitivity analyses.
Risk Factors extraction heuristics and volatility outlier filtering (±3σ) not validated; could bias features/labels.
Temporal selection of 2012–2015 chosen post-hoc based on centroids may introduce optimistic bias unless validated on fully held-out future-year data.
alternative_interpretations: Reported improvements may partially result from preprocessing/representation leakage: embedding and PCA fitted on entire dataset could allow information from test folds to influence features, inflating performance.
Performance gains attributed to embedding-augmentation might instead be due to better hyperparameter choices (PCA dims, SVM kernel) or lexicon variant (LexExt) rather than the t̂cdi mechanism per se.
Temporal selection (2012–2015) could reduce heterogeneity and make the task easier; improvement may reflect in-sample concentration rather than a universally better feature construction.
Sector-specific underperformance could stem from domain mismatch (features not capturing sector-specific risk semantics) or overfitting in low-data regimes, not solely sample size.
transparency_notes: Please state whether Word2Vec embeddings and PCA were trained inside each CV fold (only on training folds) or once on the entire dataset. If the latter, re-run time-ordered/within-fold training to avoid leakage.

Provide full Word2Vec training hyperparameters (vector size, window, negative sampling, epochs, seed) and PCA fitting details (whitening, centering), plus whether random seeds were fixed for reproducibility.

Publish per-fold results, CI estimates, and code/data (anonymized link provided in manuscript) to enable replication; clarify Risk Factors extraction heuristics and supply a small manual annotation for extraction validation.
Describe the exact stacking protocol (which models as base learners, meta-feature normalization, cross-validation within stacking) and report sensitivity to the 70%-30% split.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although the core technical idea (embedding-augmented IR weighting) is drawn from IR literature (Rekabsaz et al.), its transfer to long-form sentiment features for financial volatility forecasting appears novel in this combination—this is an innovation signal but does not imply empirical validity without the robustness checks noted.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If Word2Vec embeddings are trained solely on past (training-fold) data and similarity thresholds optimally tuned, the embedding-augmented counts could robustly capture semantic variants of lexicon terms and lead to consistent r2 improvements across folds.
If PCA is fit only on training data and SVM hyperparameters are properly tuned per method, the reported gains may persist and statistical tests will confirm significance.
If Risk Factors extraction is accurate (high precision/recall), then text features will be less noisy and embedding-augmentation is more likely to add genuine semantic signal rather than noise.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Method reuses known embedding-augmented IR weighting (Rekabsaz et al.) and lexicon-expansion concepts (Tsai & Wang) but applies them cohesively to long 10-K Risk Factors with fusion to market features and sector/temporal analyses—this is an incremental yet useful adaptation.
evidence: Method section explicitly cites Rekabsaz and Tsai; experiments compare against Tsai and Wang baselines.
uncertainty_flags: Robustness and generalizability of empirical gains remain to be demonstrated (stat tests, leakage prevention).

novelty_lenses.rationale: The conceptual pipeline is sound and plausible, but critical methodological issues (leakage risk, missing CIs, underreported hyperparam choices) limit confidence in the empirical claims.
evidence: Clear pipeline (eq.3, PCA, SVM, stacking) but lack of transparency about embedding/PCA within-CV fitting.
uncertainty_flags: High until authors provide re-runs/clarifications ensuring no leakage and add statistical reporting.

confidence_interval.rationale: I have medium confidence that the proposed embedding-augmented weighting offers real predictive improvement (supported by reported point estimates and coherent method). However, missing statistical uncertainty, possible leakage in representation learning, and absent sensitivity analyses materially reduce confidence. If the authors address major methodological concerns (M1, M2, M3) and show significance and robustness, confidence would rise substantially.

consensus_findings: Embedding-augmented IR weighting (t̂cdi propagated into standard schemes, e.g., B̂M25) is a coherent and well-specified methodological adaptation from IR to lexicon-based sentiment for long 10-K Risk Factors and yields point-estimate improvements in reported r2 relative to standard weightings and prior lexicon-expansion baselines on the authors' experimental setup.

Combining textual features with market features via late fusion (stacking) produced higher point-estimate predictive performance and visually slower decay across longer prediction horizons in the presented experiments compared to market-only or text-only baselines.

The manuscript presents substantial empirical work: multiple weighting schemes (standard and 'hat' variants), lexicon variants (Lex, LexExt), fusion strategies (early fusion, MKL, stacking), temporal/sector analyses, and comparisons to prior baselines (Wang, Tsai) and market baselines (GARCH, Market).

Temporal heterogeneity is observed in the dataset: year-centroid cosine-similarity analysis indicates multi-year clustering and the authors' selection of a recent-year window (2012–2015) is motivated by improved cross-validated performance.

Sectoral analyses reveal interpretable term-sense differences across sectors; reported underperformance of sector-specific models relative to a general model is plausibly linked to limited per-sector training data in the current dataset.
disagreements: Magnitude and robustness of the reported predictive improvements: reviewers agree point estimates favor the proposed pipeline, but disagree (or remain cautious) about whether the improvements are statistically robust and generalize beyond the provided CV setup because confidence intervals and significance tests are missing.

Severity of potential temporal/data leakage: reviewers uniformly flagged leakage risks (Word2Vec and PCA training on full corpus, CV fold construction), but differ on how likely such leakage materially inflates results without access to implementation details; some reviewers consider it a major immediate risk requiring re-run, others classify it as plausible but remediable with clarifications.

Interpretation of sector-specific underperformance: reviewers concur that limited sample size is a likely driver but disagree whether current experiments sufficiently isolate sample-size effects from other causes (overfitting, feature mismatch, sector encoding). Some request learning curves and transfer tests to resolve this.

Novelty framing: all reviewers treat the technical move as an incremental adaptation (embedding-augmented IR → sentiment features). A subset emphasizes it as an interesting innovation signal given sparse direct precedents in volatility forecasting literature, whereas others regard it as an expected transfer with limited theoretical novelty.
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical uncertainty: absence of per-fold metrics, standard deviations, confidence intervals, and paired hypothesis tests for key r2/MSE comparisons (hat vs non-hat, stacking vs MKL/early fusion, text+market vs baselines).

Representation-learning leakage: unclear whether Word2Vec embeddings and PCA were trained exclusively within training folds (no leakage) or on the full dataset (risking leakage of future information into features).

Hyperparameter and sensitivity dependence: lack of reported ablations for Word2Vec hyperparameters (dim, window, epochs), similarity threshold (0.70), neighbor counts (top-k), PCA dimensionality (400), and SVM hyperparameters—results may be sensitive to these choices.

Temporal generalization: reliance on 5-fold CV within a 2012–2015 subset and post-hoc selection of that window raises concern about temporal selection bias; limited forward-year holdouts shown but not exhaustive rolling-origin experiments.

Risk Factors extraction and label filtering: extraction heuristics for Item 1A and volatility outlier filtering (mean ± 3σ) are under-validated; mis-extraction or removal of informative extremes could bias feature quality and evaluation.

Marginal attribution: interactions among LexExt expansion, t̂cdi weighting, PCA, and SVM-RBF are entangled; the marginal contribution of the embedding-augmented weighting relative to other pipeline components is insufficiently isolated.
model_diversity_effects: Across specialist reviewers, model diversity yielded complementary emphases: structure-focused reviewers highlighted logical chain and experimental coverage; methodology auditors emphasized reproducibility and leakage risks; novelty assessors stressed incremental innovation value but demanded robustness evidence. These role-specific perspectives converged on the same methodological blind spots (statistics, leakage, sensitivity) but differed in weight and suggested remedies.

Diverse reviewer roles helped surface both technical and practical concerns: for example, novelty assessors accepted adaptation novelty but method auditors insisted on nested-validation and time-aware splits; this combination sharpens the set of required reproducibility checks.

The ensemble of reviewer perspectives increases confidence that the reported empirical signal is plausible (innovation signal plus point-estimate gains) while simultaneously identifying the narrow set of methodological controls that most influence credibility (training-of-embedding/PCA within folds, CI/statistics, and hyperparameter sweeps).
meta_review.editor_guidance: Focus editorial assessment on methodological robustness and reproducibility rather than novelty judgment. Request the authors to (1) clarify and, if necessary, re-run core experiments ensuring no representation-learning leakage: train Word2Vec and PCA only on training data within each CV or on past-only data for temporal splits; (2) report per-fold results, standard deviations, and 95% confidence intervals and perform paired statistical tests for principal comparisons (B̂M25 vs BM25, stacking vs MKL/early fusion, Text+Market vs Market); (3) supply sensitivity analyses for embedding/expansion hyperparameters (similarity threshold, neighbor counts), PCA dimensionality, and SVM hyperparameter tuning (prefer nested CV or a held-out validation protocol); (4) validate Risk Factors extraction accuracy on a manually annotated sample and report the impact of volatility outlier filtering (with/without extremes); and (5) provide code, fixed random seeds, and precise data-split descriptions (including any company-level or temporal partitioning) to permit reproduction. These checks will enable a central decision grounded in methodological validity and generalization evidence.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidentiary claims and reproducibility, please provide (and ideally re-run) the following: (A) Explicit pipeline ordering and training protocol showing that Word2Vec and PCA were fit only on training data within each cross-validation fold or, for temporal experiments, only on historical training years—if fits were previously done on full data, re-run without leakage. (B) Per-fold r2 and MSE numbers, sample sizes per fold, standard deviations/standard errors, and bootstrap or paired statistical tests (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank) for the main method vs closest baselines; add error bands to quartile and sector plots. (C) Ablation/sensitivity studies: vary similarity threshold (e.g., 0.60/0.70/0.80), neighbor counts (5/10/20/50), at least one alternative embedding (e.g., fastText or pretrained financial embeddings), PCA dims (100, 200, 400, 800), and SVM hyperparameters (grid search with nested CV), reporting effects on mean and variance of metrics. (D) Risk Factors extraction validation: a small manual annotation (e.g., 50–200 filings) reporting extraction precision/recall and an experiment showing model performance with and without outlier filtering. (E) Learning-curve and transfer experiments for sector analysis to disentangle sample-size effects from domain mismatch (and consider alternative sector encodings beyond one-hot). (F) Release code, seeds, full hyperparameter grids, and exact data-split definitions (or scripts to recreate splits) to enable replication. Present these additions clearly (tables/plots) and adjust claims' language to reflect statistical significance and observed robustness ranges.
transparency_report: All reviewers flagged missing implementation details: Word2Vec training hyperparameters (vector size, window, epochs, negative sampling), whether embeddings were trained per-fold or on the full corpus, PCA fitting protocol (fit per-fold or globally, whitening), and random seeds for reproducibility are not fully reported.

Evaluation transparency: Tables and figures present only point estimates (mean r2/MSE) without per-fold variance or confidence intervals; no paired statistical tests are reported for main comparisons.

Data-preprocessing transparency gaps: Risk Factors extraction heuristics are described at a high level (term matching and HTML cleaning) but no quantitative accuracy of extraction is provided; volatility outlier filtering (mean ± 3σ) is stated without counts of removed examples or sensitivity checks.

Fusion and training protocol: stacking split ratios and the set of base learners are described but meta-model training details (cross-validation within stacking, normalization of meta-features) and whether representation learning was nested are unclear.

Reproducibility artifacts: dataset availability is referenced (anonymous URL) but code for feature construction (t̂cdi implementation), embedding/PCA training scripts, and experiment orchestration are not attached in the main text; reviewers recommend providing code and exact seeds.
epistemic_limits: The synthesis is bounded by the reviewers' access to the manuscript text and reported summary tables/figures rather than raw code or outputs; we cannot determine whether representation-learning steps were actually fit inside training folds or on the full dataset without author confirmation—this is the single largest epistemic uncertainty affecting credibility. Reported numerical improvements are point estimates from the authors' CV experiments; absence of confidence intervals and formal tests prevents adjudicating statistical significance here. Sensitivity to embedding/PCA/SVM hyperparameters and to Risk Factors extraction remains unknown until ablations or re-runs are provided. Finally, generalization beyond the 2012–2015 window and to truly out-of-sample future years (post-2015) is unverified; temporal selection may have improved in-sample CV performance while reducing out-of-time generalizability. These limits imply that the presented empirical gains should be treated as plausible but provisional until the methodological remediation steps (leakage control, CI/statistics, hyperparameter/sensitivity analyses, extraction validation, code release) are completed and their outcomes reported.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript adapts embedding-augmented IR term-weighting (propagating cosine-weighted Word2Vec neighbor counts into TC/TF/TFIDF/BM25) to produce lexicon-driven sentiment features from 10-K Item 1A Risk Factors, reduces dimensions with PCA, uses SVM-RBF regressors, and fuses text with market features (early fusion, MKL, stacking). On the authors' 2012–2015 subset and 5-fold cross-validation, embedding-extended weightings (notably B̂M25) and stacking Text+Market report higher point r2 and visually slower decay across longer forecast horizons than prior lexicon baselines (Wang 2013, Tsai & Wang 2014) and market/GARCH baselines. Reviewers find the methodological transfer coherent and the empirical scope broad (weighting/fusion/temporal/sector analyses), but identify substantive gaps in statistical uncertainty reporting, potential representation-learning/temporal leakage, and sensitivity/reproducibility checks that limit confidence in generalization.
strengths: Clear, mechanistic adaptation of embedding-aware IR weighting (t̂cdi formulation) from retrieval literature (Rekabsaz et al.) to lexicon-based sentiment for long documents; equations and pipeline are explicitly described.

Comprehensive empirical comparisons: multiple weighting schemes (standard and 'hat' variants), lexicon variants (Lex, LexExt), fusion strategies (early fusion, MKL via mklaren, stacking), and relevant baselines (GARCH/Market; Wang 2013; Tsai & Wang 2014).

Temporal and sectoral characterization: year-centroid clustering used to motivate a recent-year training window (2012–2015) and sector analyses reveal interpretable term-sense differences and sample-size effects.
limitations: Absence of statistical uncertainty reporting: core results are presented as point estimates (mean r2/MSE) without per-fold variances, confidence intervals, or paired statistical tests to assess robustness of improvements (e.g., B̂M25 vs BM25, stacking vs MKL/early fusion).

Potential representation-learning and temporal leakage: Word2Vec and PCA training procedures relative to cross-validation/temporal splits are not clearly documented. If embeddings/PCA were fit on the full corpus prior to CV, features could leak future information into training and inflate performance estimates.

Underreported sensitivity and ablation analyses: key hyperparameters that materially affect the embedding-augmentation (Word2Vec hyperparameters, similarity threshold 0.70, top-k neighbor counts for LexExt), PCA dimensionality (400), and SVM kernel/hyperparameter selection lack systematic tuning or robustness checks.

Risk-factor extraction and label-processing validation missing: extraction of Item 1A Risk Factors via heuristics and removal of volatility outliers (mean ± 3σ) are operational choices that are not validated against manual annotations, and their impact on feature quality and label distribution is not quantified.
open_questions: Were Word2Vec embeddings and PCA fitted strictly within each training fold (or trained only on past data for temporal splits)? If not, please re-run experiments with embeddings/PCA trained exclusively on training data and report differences.

Can the authors provide per-fold r2 and MSE values (or bootstrap 95% CIs) and run paired tests (e.g., Wilcoxon or paired t-test) for the principal comparisons (B̂M25 vs BM25; Text+Market stacking vs Market baseline; stacking vs MKL)?

How sensitive are results to the embedding-expansion hyperparameters: similarity threshold, number of neighbors in LexExt, and Word2Vec training choices (vector size, window, epochs)? Please report ablations (e.g., thresholds 0.60/0.70/0.80 and neighbor counts 5/10/20/50).

What is the precision/recall of the Risk Factors extraction heuristics on a manual sample, and how many volatility samples were removed by the mean ± 3σ filtering? Provide model performance with and without this filtering to assess biasing effects.
consensus_snapshot: Embedding-augmented IR weighting (t̂cdi → hat-weightings like B̂M25) is a coherent, plausible adaptation and yields consistent point-estimate improvements over standard weightings in the reported experiments.
Stacking (late fusion) combining text and market modalities shows higher point-estimate r2 and appears to reduce long-horizon performance decay versus market-only baselines in the provided plots.
The manuscript provides an extensive empirical landscape (weightings, lexicon variants, fusion methods, temporal/sector experiments) that is valuable to the community as a comparative study.
disagreement_snapshot: Reviewers agree on the plausibility of the main methodological move but disagree on how much of the reported numerical improvement is attributable to that move versus other pipeline choices (PCA dimension, SVM tuning, LexExt) or potential leakage. Some reviewers view missing procedural details as a major threat requiring re-run; others treat them as remediable clarifications that, once provided, will likely preserve the core findings.

There is no disagreement that statistical uncertainty must be reported; disagreement lies in the assessed immediacy of re-running experiments versus first receiving clarifications (i.e., whether current numbers are likely severely biased or only tentatively optimistic).
uncertainty_snapshot: Key epistemic uncertainty centers on whether representation learning steps (Word2Vec, PCA) were fit within training folds: if they were not, reported r2 may be optimistic.

Lack of CIs and fold-level dispersion introduces ambiguity about the statistical significance and effect-size stability of improvements; point differences (e.g., Text r2 0.439 vs Tsai 0.395) could be within sampling noise.
Unexplored sensitivity to embedding/expansion hyperparameters and PCA dims leaves open whether the method generalizes across reasonable implementation choices and to future-year out-of-sample data.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The manuscript adapts embedding-augmented IR weighting (t̂cdi) to construct lexicon-based sentiment features from 10-K Risk Factors, applies PCA and SVM-RBF, and fuses text with market features (stacking, MKL, early fusion). On a 2012–2015 subset and 5-fold CV, hat-weightings (notably B̂M25) and stacking Text+Market show higher point r2 and appear to stabilize long-horizon forecasts versus prior lexicon approaches and market/GARCH baselines. The pipeline is coherent and the empirical breadth (weightings, lexicon variants, fusion, temporal/sectoral analyses) is a practical contribution.

Strengths:
- Principled methodological transfer: embedding-augmented IR weighting (eq.3) is clearly specified and plausibly suited for long, redundant 10-K Risk Factors (cites Rekabsaz et al.).
- Broad empirical exploration: systematic comparisons across weighting formulas, lexicon variants, fusion strategies, and baselines provide useful benchmarking data.
- Dataset characterization: year-centroid clustering and sectoral term analyses give interpretive context and operational insights (training-window selection, term-sense disambiguation).

Limitations:
- Missing statistical uncertainty: no per-fold variances, confidence intervals, or paired hypothesis tests are reported for key r2/MSE comparisons, limiting claims about significance and robustness.
- Potential representation-learning/temporal leakage: unclear whether Word2Vec and PCA were trained only on training folds or on full corpus; training on full data would leak future information and bias results upward.
- Limited sensitivity analyses: core hyperparameters (similarity threshold 0.70, neighbor count for LexExt, Word2Vec settings, PCA dims, SVM tuning) are not comprehensively ablated, leaving open whether gains generalize across reasonable settings.
- Under-validated data preprocessing: Risk Factors extraction heuristics and volatility outlier filtering (mean ± 3σ) lack manual validation and sensitivity checks; both can affect feature purity and label distribution.

Open Questions:
1) Confirm whether Word2Vec embeddings and PCA were fitted exclusively on training data (within folds or past-only splits). If not, please re-run without leakage and report revised metrics. 
2) Provide per-fold r2/MSE and 95% CIs and run paired tests for main contrasts (B̂M25 vs BM25, stacking vs MKL/early fusion, Text+Market vs Market). 
3) Supply ablation results for similarity thresholds (e.g., 0.6/0.7/0.8), neighbor counts (5/10/20/50), and an alternative embedding (fastText or pretrained financial embeddings) to assess sensitivity. 
4) Report Risk Factors extraction accuracy on a manually annotated sample (precision/recall) and show model performance with and without volatility outlier filtering, plus count of removed samples.

Transparency:
The manuscript gives clear high-level methods and formulas but omits implementation specifics critical for reproducibility: Word2Vec training params and whether trained per-fold; PCA fitting protocol (fit per-fold or global); per-fold metrics/CIs; exact Risk Factors extraction rules and extraction-validation sample; full hyperparameter search details; and code/seed release. Reviewers request these artifacts and clarifications.

confidence_interval.rationale: Moderate confidence that the methodological adaptation is valid and that point-estimate improvements are plausible given the reported experiments and prior IR literature (Rekabsaz et al.) and comparisons to Tsai & Wang and Wang baselines. However, substantial uncertainty remains because of missing statistical uncertainty, possible representation-learning/temporal leakage, and absent sensitivity analyses; these issues could materially change numeric effect sizes. The interval reflects this mixture of plausibility and methodological uncertainty.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
